title: The Quiet House
premise: When Gideon Whitlock returns to the family house to bury his twin brother Ambrose, he discovers the body in the casket is wearing his own face — and no one else seems to notice. The excavation crew hired to dig a new foundation unearths a door sealed from the inside, and the moment it opens, they are pulled into 1974, into the year Gideon's father made a bargain that split one boy into two. To escape, they must return what was taken — the original child, still alive behind the door, sustained by stolen memories — but every memory they give back erases someone who carried it. In the end, Gideon must choose between remaining himself or becoming the whole person his father destroyed, and he chooses dissolution: the house falls quiet at last because there is finally only one Whitlock left, and he remembers everything.
about_author: Cyrus Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing estate sales in rural New England before turning to fiction. He writes in longhand and claims never to reread his own books once published.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face
chapters.summary: Gideon arrives at the Whitlock house for his brother's funeral and finds the open casket holding a corpse with his own face, down to the scar on the chin. Told from Gideon's POV through his compulsive documentation habit. The emotional beat is uncanny denial — he photographs everything, as if evidence could make the impossible behave.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Gideon interviews the funeral director, who insists the body is Ambrose's and grows strangely agitated by Gideon's notebook. Flashbacks establish the twins' childhood silence around their father's locked study. POV alternates between Gideon and the director's fragmented recollection. The beat is creeping isolation: the world agrees on a story only Gideon knows is false.

chapters.title: Groundbreaking
chapters.summary: The excavation crew — foreman Dana Okafor, surveyor Pete, and young laborer Marcus — begins digging the new foundation while Gideon catalogs the house's sealed rooms. Dana notices the soil resists in one precise rectangle, as if something beneath refuses to be moved. POV shifts to Dana. The beat is professional unease hardening into dread.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: The crew unearths a steel door set flush into bedrock, its bolts thrown from within, hinges fused with rust that analysis dates to 1974. Gideon recognizes the door from a childhood nightmare. Told from Dana's POV with Gideon observing. The beat is awe curdling into violation — a grave dug upward instead of down.

chapters.title: What the Bolts Remember
chapters.summary: Pete cuts the bolts; the moment the door cracks, every person on site hears their own name spoken in a child's voice. Marcus faints; the dogs refuse the property line. Gideon finds his father's journal hidden in the study wall, dated the week of the sealing. POV: Gideon. The beat is the past asserting itself — the house has been waiting.

chapters.title: The Journal of Edmund Whitlock
chapters.summary: Through journal excerpts and Gideon's present-day annotations, we learn Edmund conducted rituals to 'consolidate' his sons after a drowning accident, splitting one child into two and entombing the original behind the door. POV is epistolary, Edmund's voice bleeding into Gideon's marginalia. The beat is horrified inheritance — Gideon realizes he may be the copy.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Marcus, clearing debris near the open door, steps through and vanishes; when Dana reaches in to grab him, both are pulled inside and find themselves in the house as it stood in 1974, wallpaper fresh, Edmund alive at his desk. POV: Dana. The beat is vertigo — the door doesn't lead anywhere; it leads whenever.

chapters.title: The Boy Behind the Door
chapters.summary: In 1974, Dana and Marcus encounter the original child — whole, terrified, and impossibly old-eyed — who begs them not to let 'the others' feed again. Back in the present, Gideon hears them shouting through the door seam. POV splits between Dana and Gideon across the threshold. The beat is compassion meeting helplessness.

chapters.title: Feed
chapters.summary: Gideon understands the mechanism: the original survives on memories given willingly, and each gift strengthens the door's pull. Pete, grieving his dead daughter, offers a memory of her and comes back younger-eyed, unable to recall her name. POV: Pete. The beat is grief weaponized — the house accepts payment and asks for more.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Self
chapters.summary: Gideon begins cataloguing his own memories, ranking what he could afford to lose, and discovers gaps already carved out — childhood summers, his mother's face — consumed years ago without his knowledge. POV: Gideon, increasingly unreliable. The beat is identity horror: he cannot verify which recollections are truly his.

chapters.title: Ambrose Wakes
chapters.summary: The buried twin's body disappears from the funeral home; that night Ambrose appears in the house, solid, warm, insisting he is the real brother and Gideon is the interment. POV: Ambrose, charming and wrong. The beat is gaslit terror — the reader can no longer be certain which twin narrates truthfully.

chapters.title: The Consolidation
chapters.summary: Edmund's journal reveals the ritual's final phase: the two copies must merge over the original's body, restoring one complete child and erasing both brothers as they exist. Dana and Marcus, trapped in 1974, discover Edmund preparing the same room they now stand in. POV: Dana. The beat is converging doom across fifty years.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Dana bargains with the original child: if she carries him out, he will show her the way back. He names what was taken in 1974 — not an object, but a person's wholeness, divisible and transferable. Marcus refuses to leave without giving the child one true memory first. POV: Marcus. The beat is sacrifice offered freely, unlike Pete's grief-driven trade.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: The crew learns the door will close forever at the autumn equinox, taking everyone inside with it unless the original is restored to the living world and the copies surrender their claim. Gideon, reading the final journal pages, finds Edmund's confession: he did it to avoid burying a son, and buried three people instead. POV: Gideon. The beat is moral clarity arriving too late to be comfortable.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: The town's lights brown out; the house exhales cold; Ambrose grows translucent as the deadline nears, revealing he was always more echo than man. Gideon and Ambrose confront each other in the nursery, each holding the other's oldest memory. POV alternates rapidly between twins. The beat is fraternal reckoning — hatred dissolving into shared grief.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Gideon enters the door deliberately, joining Dana and Marcus in 1974, where Edmund — younger, monstrous in his tenderness — mistakes him for his own son and embraces him. The original child hides in the cellar among jars labeled with names. POV: Gideon. The beat is the seduction of being loved by the thing that ruined you.

chapters.title: Jars
chapters.summary: In the cellar, the crew finds hundreds of jars of preserved memory, including Edmund's own — guilt, love, fear — extracted so he could perform fatherhood without feeling it. Dana smashes her father's jar, found among them, and feels nothing where love should be. POV: Dana. The beat is power's corruption laid bare: Edmund amputated his own heart to keep control.

chapters.title: The Bargain Reversed
chapters.summary: Gideon offers the original child everything: his memories, his name, his claim on existence. The child refuses to take unwillingly what was taken from him by force, and instead asks Gideon to choose freely, one memory at a time, until only the essential remains. POV: Gideon. The beat is agency reclaimed — the anti-ritual, consent as exorcism.

chapters.title: One Memory at a Time
chapters.summary: A montage-like chapter of surrenders: first languages, then faces, then the funeral, then Ambrose himself, each loss rendered in luminous specific detail. Dana and Marcus carry the weakening child toward the door as the house screams. POV rotates among all four. The beat is elegiac — dissolution as an act of love rather than defeat.

chapters.title: The Quiet House
chapters.summary: At the threshold, the original child becomes whole and walks out into the present as the sole surviving Whitlock, while Gideon's last retained memory — his mother singing — passes into him like light into glass. The door seals itself from the outside this time. POV: the restored child, disoriented and complete. The beat is terrible peace.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the crew testifies to nothing anyone believes; the house stands empty and genuinely quiet for the first time in fifty years. The restored Whitlock, bearing fragments of Gideon, Dana, and Marcus alongside his own recovered self, buries two small coffins side by side. POV: the restored child. The beat is mourning without resolution — some debts are paid, not forgiven.

chapters.title: Prayer, Answered
chapters.summary: In the final scene, the survivor finds Gideon's notebooks in the study wall and reads his own life documented in a stranger's hand, then adds a final entry: 'Someone remembered me. That was enough.' He leaves the notebook for whoever digs next. POV: the survivor. The beat is haunted hope — documentation as prayer, and prayer, at last, answered.
